name: Collapsing Global Texture
description: A spherical configuration of four scalar fields collapsing under its own gradients. Its gravitational field has a solid angle deficit that grows as the collapse approaches. The metric is known explicitly to first order in the field's gravitational strength; the full self similar solution is determined numerically.
convention: We use $c=\hbar=1$, so $t$ and $r$ are lengths, and a dot denotes differentiation with respect to an affine parameter. The full solution has $ds^2=-dt^2+dr^2+r^2\omega^2(u)d\Omega^2$, where $u=t/r$, $d\Omega^2=d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2$, $\chi=f(u)$, and primes denote $d/du$. It satisfies $(1-u^2)(\omega^2f')'+\sin(2f)=0$, $\omega''=-(\epsilon/2)\omega(f')^2$, and $(u\omega'-\omega)^2-(\omega')^2+(\epsilon/2)(1-u^2)\omega^2(f')^2+\epsilon\sin^2f=1$ [durrer1992textures].
history: Four scalar fields with a fixed combined magnitude have a three sphere of possible values [durrer1992textures]. Their direction can vary across space, forming a global texture whose gradients drive it to collapse. For a spherical texture, one angle $\chi(t,r)$ describes the field's direction, and the self similar collapse has the same profile at each scale. The four component field is $\vec{\phi}=\eta(\sin\chi\,\hat{r},\cos\chi)$, where $\eta$ is its fixed magnitude and $\hat{r}$ the radial unit vector.¶Dirk Nötzold calculated the gravitational field of a collapsing spherical texture in 1991 to first order in $\epsilon=8\pi G\eta^2$ [noetzold1991textures]. Nötzold used the proper time and radial distance of a flat background, with the geometry's time dependence in the areas of spheres about the centre. Manuel Barriola and Tanmay Vachaspati calculated the coupled metric and scalar field that year [barriola1991strong]. Barriola and Vachaspati also obtained analytical approximations to the metric in comoving coordinates [barriola1991approx]. Ruth Durrer, Markus Heusler, Philippe Jetzer, and Norbert Straumann also studied the coupled Einstein and scalar field equations in 1991 [durrer1991collapse]. Durrer and coauthors developed the solution in two coordinate systems in 1992 and related those systems by a coordinate transformation [durrer1992textures].¶The collapse occurs at $t=0$. Before collapse, the similarity variable is $x=-t/r>0$, and the angular function is $w(x)=-2+2x\arctan(1/x)$ [noetzold1991textures]. Through first order, the line element is $ds^2=-dt^2+dr^2+r^2H(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2)$, with $H=1+\epsilon w(x)$. Durrer and coauthors expressed the same angular factor through $y=r/t=-1/x$: $\omega=1+\epsilon[\arctan(y)/y-1]$, with $H=\omega^2+O(\epsilon^2)$ [durrer1992textures].¶A sphere at proper radial distance $r$ has area $4\pi r^2H$. Its remaining solid angle is $4\pi H$, and its missing solid angle is $\Delta\Omega=-4\pi\epsilon w(x)$ [noetzold1991textures]. At a fixed nonzero $r$, the missing angle grows from zero in the distant past toward $8\pi\epsilon$ as $t\to0^-$. The change is self similar: spheres with the same $-t/r$ have the same deficit.¶Nötzold stated that test matter feels no gravitational force unless it has angular momentum about the texture's centre [noetzold1991textures]. In these coordinates radial geodesics obey $\ddot t=\ddot r=0$, and a particle initially at rest retains its radial coordinate. The shrinking spatial volume still increases the density of initially uniform dust, with its density proportional to $H^{-1}$ [durrer1992textures]. The dust is treated as test matter, with its own gravitational field neglected.¶For the nonlinear solution, Durrer and colleagues use $u=t/r$, $\chi=f(u)$ and the angular factor $\omega^2(u)$, solving coupled ordinary differential equations by shooting [durrer1992textures]. The nonlinear geometry describes the field outside the small core in which its magnitude changes during unwinding. The fixed magnitude sigma model cannot resolve that event. Nötzold gives several post collapse continuations, so a continuation through the unwinding requires additional physical assumptions [noetzold1991textures].¶Barriola evolved the full scalar field equations numerically in 1993 to follow the field after collapse [barriola1993collapse]. Albert Stebbins and Shoba Veeraraghavan calculated the microwave temperature pattern of an isolated spherical texture over the full sky in 1995 [stebbins1995sky]. The weak field temperature pattern loses the symmetry between the hot and cold phases; smoothing with a telescope beam leaves a deeper cold extremum. Stefan Åminneborg and Lars Bergström examined the self similar approximation in expanding cosmological backgrounds in 1995 [aminneborg1995textures]. A spherical texture on a fixed radiation or matter dominated flat background has no nontrivial exactly self similar profile that crosses the similarity horizon smoothly. Åminneborg and Bergström also found numerical evidence for additional flat space profiles, distinguished by their oscillations about $\chi=\pi/2$.¶Eduardo Guéron and Patricio S. Letelier followed test particles through the weak gravitational field of a spherical texture in 1997 [gueron1997newtonian]. The particles first concentrate and then disperse in their Newtonian model. André Luis Batista Ribeiro and Letelier derived a collapse criterion for surrounding matter in 1999 [ribeiro1999bound]. A spherical over density becomes bound when its initial radius lies below a critical radius set by the symmetry breaking scale and cosmological density.¶Owen Dando coupled the spherical texture to a dilaton in 1999 [dando1999dilaton]. Dando found self similar collapse with a massless dilaton and a modified deficit in the surrounding geometry. The dilaton rescales the Einstein metric to the string metric; curvature in the string metric diverges on the past light cone unless the dilaton coupling takes the decoupling value ($a=-1$). A dilaton mass introduces a length scale and generally breaks this self similarity.¶Piotr Bizoń and Arthur Wasserman included gravitational backreaction in 2000 and found numerical evidence for a countable family of spherical self similar solutions [bizon2000wave]. The gravitational coupling is $\alpha=\epsilon/2$ in their normalization. Sascha Husa, Christiane Lechner, Michael Pürrer, Jonathan Thornburg, and Peter C. Aichelburg found discrete self similarity at the black hole threshold in 2000 [husa2000critical]. Near this threshold, the field profile repeats after a discrete contraction of space and time.¶Lechner and coauthors found a transition between continuous and discrete self similarity at the black hole threshold in 2002 [lechner2002transition]. Near the transition, a collapsing field repeatedly approaches and leaves a continuously self similar profile. Bizoń and Wasserman proved that a countable family exists for $0\leq\alpha<1/2$ later that year; each member is analytic from the centre to the past light cone of the central singularity [bizon2002wave]. The central singularity is naked at sufficiently small $\alpha$, with finite curvature on its future light cone.¶Bizoń, Sebastian J. Szybka, and Wasserman found an unstable periodic orbit of the reduced self similar equations beyond the past light cone in 2004 [bizon2004periodic]. Its stable manifold separates solutions that reach a future similarity horizon from solutions that encounter an apparent horizon. Szybka found numerical evidence for chaotic dynamics on this boundary at intermediate gravitational coupling ($0.426\lesssim\alpha\lesssim0.482$) [szybka2004chaotic]. Szybka also found a fractal boundary between the two outcomes.¶Aichelburg, Bizoń, and Zbislaw Tabor resolved further structure near the transition between continuous and discrete self similarity in 2006 [aichelburg2006bifurcation]. Marginally supercritical fields can form two apparent horizons almost simultaneously, and the radius of the inner horizon changes discontinuously as the initial data vary. The number of approaches to the continuously self similar profile changes across these jumps. The outer horizon radius follows the discrete self similar scaling law.¶Marcos Cruz and coauthors fitted a collapsing texture to the Cold Spot in Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) data in 2007 [cruz2007coldspot]. Photons crossing the time dependent gravitational potential can acquire the temperature decrement of this cold region in the cosmic microwave background (CMB). Such a texture would also bend CMB photon trajectories.¶Cruz and coauthors compared the texture profile with five year WMAP observations in 2008 [cruz2008coldspot]. The posterior odds favoured a texture over a Gaussian microwave fluctuation by a modest factor ($2.7$). Gaussian simulations of the three year WMAP data produced comparable evidence for a texture in about $5\%$ of cases.¶Sudeep Das and David N. Spergel calculated the CMB lensing signature of a collapsing texture in 2009 [das2009lensing]. The texture acts as a converging lens, and its bending of light supplements the temperature shift of photons crossing the time dependent geometry [das2009lensing]. The deflection changes the angular correlations of the background temperature field.¶Bizoń, Tadeusz Chmaj, Andrzej Rostworowski, and Stanisław Zając calculated the late decay of wave maps coupled to gravity in 2009 [tails2009wave]. Small, compact disturbances of the vacuum in the spherical hedgehog sector decay at fixed radius as $t^{-4}$. At future null infinity, the radiation field decays as the inverse square of retarded time. The leading tail comes from gravitational self interaction.¶Patricio Vielva and coauthors used the correlation between CMB temperature and E mode polarization to distinguish a primordial Cold Spot from a secondary texture signal in 2011 [vielva2011polarization]. A gravitational temperature shift from the texture does not carry the primordial temperature and polarization correlation. Ben Rathaus, Anastasia Fialkov, and Nissan Itzhaki recalculated the temperature lensing forecast that year [rathaus2011lens]. The texture parameters fitted to WMAP produced a lensing signal below the fluctuations from intervening cosmological structure.¶Stephen M. Feeney and coauthors searched the full sky WMAP seven year data for a population of texture temperature profiles in 2012 [feeney2012constraint]. They found no statistical preference for adding textures. Feeney and coauthors refined the search with filters matched to the texture profile in 2013 [feeney2013hierarchical]. They bounded the expected number of detectable textures on the full sky ($<5.2$ at $95\%$ confidence), for angular scales from $2^\circ$ to $50^\circ$ and fractional temperature amplitudes from $2.5\times10^{-5}$ to $10^{-4}$.¶Ely D. Kovetz and Marc Kamionkowski forecast the lensing of redshifted hydrogen radiation by a texture in 2013 [kovetz2013lensing]. A texture near redshift six would be difficult to detect with the Square Kilometre Array specifications they considered. Raúl Fernández-Cobos and coauthors adapted the polarization test to observations covering part of the sky that year [fernandez2013polarization]. The radial and tangential polarization patterns retain information about the correlation with temperature. The WMAP nine year polarization data were too noisy to distinguish a primordial Cold Spot from a secondary temperature signal.¶Robert Brandenberger and Hao Jiao estimated the abundance of matter concentrations seeded by collapsing textures in 2020 [brandenberger2020seeds]. At cosmologically allowed symmetry breaking scales, the texture unwinds before its energy is enclosed by a black hole horizon. The surrounding matter can retain a nonlinear over density that seeds later accretion. Brandenberger, Bryce Cyr, and Jiao also calculated photon and neutrino emission from unwinding textures in 2020 [brandenberger2020rays]. The emitted photons can distort the CMB spectrum; the predicted amplitudes depend on the fraction of the released energy carried by photons.¶Marzieh Farhang and coauthors fitted the texture temperature and lensing profiles jointly to Planck data in 2021 [farhang2021coldspot]. The fitted temperature amplitude depends on the angular extent of the selected region, and the texture profile fails to reproduce the surrounding hot ring. They found no lensing detection; the upper bound remained consistent with the temperature fit.¶Pedro da Silveira Ferreira and Stephen Owusu combined temperature and polarization correlations to forecast this lensing signal in 2026 [ferreira2026lensing]. A texture with the parameters fitted to Planck 2018 temperature data would produce a weak lensing signal for Simons Observatory survey specifications (signal to noise ratio $1.5$). At the upper amplitude allowed by the $2\sigma$ temperature constraint, the expected ratio rises ($2.3$). The polarization channels increase the expected signal to noise ratio (about $67\%$).

related.text: A spherical defect with a solid angle deficit. The monopole's far field is static; the texture's deficit changes during collapse [noetzold1991textures].
Both are defects associated with broken symmetries. A straight string has a fixed missing angle around its axis; the texture has a changing missing solid angle about its centre [durrer1992textures].
Both scalar fields collapse self similarly. Roberts has one unconstrained massless scalar; the texture has four components constrained to a three sphere [durrer1992textures].
